meta.title: Destination Analysis Explained Simply | Nick Sleep and the Nomad Letters
meta.author: Nick Sleep
meta.end: Quotations and ringed passages are from the Nomad Investment Partnership letters (Sleep, Zakaria and Company), with the letter period and PDF page shown. Lines marked “our note” are our own reading.
meta.description:
Nick Sleep's destination analysis, explained simply: why the order of returns fools us, "$1 into $16: does it matter if it takes 18 years or 22?", the Stagecoach and Conseco mistakes, the old bank manager, and three destination questions for Indian investors. From the original Nomad Investment Partnership letters.

Every ringed passage is shown on the real letter page, with the letter period and page. Lines marked "our note" are our own reading.
meta.sources:
Sources (Nomad letters, compiled edition; page = PDF page)
- Annual letter, period ended 31 Dec 2005: p.74 (reordered returns; $1 → $16; "Travelling comfortably…")
- Annual letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007: p.127 (pimply youth vs bank manager), p.128 (Stagecoach, Conseco, destination analysis, ~US$60m)
- Annual letter, period ended 31 Dec 2013: p.218 (since-inception results, unaudited, before fees)
meta.tags: destination analysis, nick sleep, long term investing, anchoring bias, selling too early, nomad investment partnership, nick sleep letters, stock market for beginners

beats.say: Here's a strange trick your brain plays. Imagine five years of returns. Plus eighty percent. Plus twenty-two. Plus ten. Plus nine. Plus one. Feels like things are going downhill, right?
Now flip the order. Plus one. Plus nine. Plus ten. Plus twenty-two. Plus eighty. Feels fantastic! Getting better every year!
But you end up with exactly the same money either way. Nick Sleep pointed this out to his investors in 2005. The order changes how we feel. It doesn't change where we end up.

scene.find: the end result (the destination) is identical
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2005 · p.74

scene.sub: Judge the road by where it ends

beats.say: That's Sleep's second big idea. Stop judging the ride. Judge where it ends.

scene.q: Stop judging the ride. Judge where it ends.

beats.say: In the same letter, Sleep asked a simple question. If you could turn one dollar into sixteen, does it matter much whether it takes eighteen years or twenty-two?

scene.find: matter if it takes 18 years or 22 years
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2005 · p.74

beats.say: He was honest that the yearly return is different. Sixteen times in eighteen years is about sixteen point seven percent a year. In twenty-two years, about thirteen point four. But reaching sixteen at all matters far more.

scene.second_label: a year, if it takes 22 years

beats.say: Then he wrote the sentence that sums up how most people invest. Travelling comfortably dominates people's thinking when they should be thinking about destinations.

scene.q: Travelling comfortably dominates people’s thinking when they should be thinking about destinations.
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2005 · p.74

beats.say: Think of a family road trip to Goa. Some stretches are smooth. Some are full of potholes. And someone in the back seat asks at every single bump: are we there yet?
Would you turn the car around because of one bad stretch? Of course not. You check one thing. Are we still on the road to Goa?

scene.q: Are we still on the road to Goa?

beats.say: Destination analysis asks the same question of a business. Not, was this quarter bumpy? But, is this company still heading where I thought it was going?

items: But: is it still heading where I thought?

beats.say: Sleep learned this the hard way, and wrote about it with rare honesty in 2007. He'd bought shares of Stagecoach, a British bus company, at fourteen pence. They rose to about ninety pence, and he sold. A success!

scene.find: shares purchased at 14p were sold at a high of around 90p
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: Except that, when he was writing, the shares traded above two pounds fifty. He'd left about one pound sixty a share on the table.

scene.after: Stagecoach share price when Sleep wrote
scene.second_label: left on the table, per share
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: Why did he sell? He'd anchored on his original analysis. At fourteen pence, all he needed was a business worth more than fourteen pence. He never asked where the business itself was heading. He put the cost at about twelve million dollars, and counting.

scene.find: anchoring on the original purchase decision analysis
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: It's like selling your plot of land the day its price doubles, and then driving past the shopping mall they built on it, every single day.

scene.q: Sold the plot. Now I drive past the mall every day.

beats.say: His second big mistake was the opposite. He held Conseco, an American financial company, too long, relying on his analysis from the day he bought it. Conseco went bankrupt. Counting what the money could have earned elsewhere, he put that cost at about ten million dollars.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: Two mistakes, one cause. In both cases, he judged the company by a snapshot taken on the day he bought it, and never updated the picture.

scene.find: static view of a firm formed at the time of purchase
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: He even joked about it, calling his two biggest mistakes, sorry, learning opportunities.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: And here's the part I love. Sleep said destination analysis became central to how they studied businesses. The Conseco lesson, he believed, kept them out of American banks before the 2008 crisis. The Stagecoach lesson helped them keep holding Amazon.

scene.find: may well have kept us out of the US banks
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: He estimated those two lessons added around sixty million dollars to Nomad's results in 2007 alone. He called it a return on prior years' losses.

scene.after: rough gain in 2007 from two old lessons (Sleep's estimate)
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.128

beats.say: Sleep gave a brilliant everyday example in the same letter. Imagine your home loan was sold to you by a young salesman on commission, and then passed on to some faraway fund.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.127

beats.say: Now imagine instead that it's still held by your local bank manager, who has known your father for fifty years. You'd feel very differently about those two loans. And so would the lender.

scene.find: who has known your Dad for fifty years
scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2007 · p.127

beats.say: The first set-up looks efficient on this year's profit statement. But its destination is disloyal customers and careless lending, roughly what happened before 2008. The second looks old-fashioned. Its destination is trust.
In India we all know that bank manager. He's the reason some families have banked at the same branch for three generations.

For any Indian company you study, ask three destination questions. One. In ten years, will customers need this business more than today, or less? Two. Is it doing things now that make that future more likely, even if they hurt this year's profit? Three. What would have to go wrong for it to end up somewhere much worse?

items: 1 · In 10 years: needed more, or less?
What would have to go wrong

beats.say: And before you sell, ask one more. Am I selling because the business changed direction, or only because it hit my old target price? That's the Stagecoach question.

scene.q: Did the business change? Or only the price?

beats.say: One. Destination analysis doesn't mean ignoring bad news. Conseco shows you must update the destination when the facts change. Two. A target price is not a destination. A target price is where you get off. Three. A bumpy ride doesn't mean a bad business.
Nomad's own yearly returns bounced around a lot. Yet by the final letter, one dollar invested at the start had become ten dollars and twenty-one cents, before fees.

scene.src: Nomad letter, period ended 31 Dec 2013 · p.218 · unaudited, before fees

beats.say: One line for your friend over chai. Don't judge the trip by the potholes. Ask where the road ends.

scene.q: Don't judge the trip by the potholes. Ask where the road ends.
